author Matt Stults
subject Remove the second bad example #6 BEFORE measuring it: zero observed incidence
It taught against writing two statements in one body. The check that stopped it
ran before a cent was spent:

  rule bodies examined across every stored response : 911
  bodies containing a statement separator           : 0

The model has never produced this failure. A control arm would score zero and
the delta would be unreadable -- exactly how the FIRST bad example #6 wasted its
first run, discovered only after paying.

The asymmetry decides it: the defect is real and reproduced, but schema.py
catches it deterministically at zero prompt budget. An example earns its place
when a CHECK CANNOT catch the thing -- true of the gloss case, which is semantic
and routed to stage-4 seat 4r; false here.

Not a blocklist. The trigger to re-propose is concrete: re-run the 911-body
count against new responses, and if incidence becomes non-zero the example has a
case.

The guard stays. The statement-count check, its controls (1..3, #count{},
"a.b") and its mutant are untouched.

Reverting is byte-identical to the version Matt already accepted, so the guard
is green on all six watched files with no new review needed.

commit 4e94355300ba71f24ff10e27df6df9825cd8209b
ordinal 122
date 2026-08-08 08:00:06 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject Q-6 reframed: a stage-1 contract gap, and D-3's escape clause is half wrong
The old reading asked whether readback-ungloss is too strict. It is not, and
relaxing it would have been the wrong fix. 14 symbols block 7 modules and NOT
ONE is glossed by any module we have translated -- every one is a predicate a
module borrows, and the contract demands a gloss only for names a clause
INTRODUCES. The accumulation the design assumes has no source.

D-3 defers corpus-wide resolution because it "resolves itself as the corpus
grows". Measured: 6 of 14 are owned by a real clause and will resolve; 6 appear
NOWHERE in the document and never can, because the model coined names whose
words are not in any clause. m0053 invented interactable_entity AND
interaction_entity for one idea and glossed neither.

And linking probably cannot find the definitions without re-reading the source:
none of the five blocking clauses carries an anchor, corpus-wide only 13 0o,
so the only information carried is name+arity -- which is measured at 20% wrong.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

----END----

commit 0fdfdda2197b0cbc1fb8d0cd6eac7abf683ddb5e
ordinal 123
date 2026-08-08 08:15:43 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject Probe: can a model map the document's concept graph? Plus a frozen prediction
The whole document, 593 clauses in 78 sections, two turns on one accumulating
transcript. $0.0253. Both turns parsed, neither near the token cap.

78/78 sections covered, 258 input concepts (165 distinct), 220 document / 38
world, 108 resolved to a producing section, 36 honestly unresolved.

Statically checkable, and it half-passes: every section id resolves (0 invalid
across turn 1, produced_by and consumed_by) but only 72 of 108 evidence phrases
appear verbatim in the section they name. The misses are quotation drift, not
invention -- right section, paraphrased line -- so it is a fixable prompt
problem, and the check working is itself the finding.

BUT it overlaps the predicates our translated modules actually borrow by 1 of 32.
The map names document-level nouns; modules name clause-level predicates. Both
right, neither the other.

Pre-registered a variant asking for PREDICATES instead of CONCEPTS, with the
falsifier written down: if overlap stays near 3

----END----

commit 7dfc3830b5e5b8291a12b43dfbffa49197876946
ordinal 124
date 2026-08-08 10:45:57 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject Experiment 3, both arms, built and rendered for review -- not yet run
Prediction failed twice. Concept-level scored 1/32 against the predicates our
translator actually coined; predicate-level scored 0/32 with 268 candidates on
the table. The pre-registered falsifier fired, so the map is a RESOLUTION TARGET
(Invariant 1 arm C, "a lookup the model never sees") rather than prompt context
(arm A).

resolve_probe.py reverses the direction: supply the names we really coined, ask
only where they are defined. Three verdicts -- document, world, coinage.

IT HAS GROUND TRUTH, which neither earlier probe had. Six of the 43 supplied
predicates appear NOWHERE in the document, verified by searching every clause
for all the words of each name. A correct run calls them coinage. The key is
never shown to the model.

TWO ARMS, and the difference is the measurement. no-gloss supplies bare names;
gloss also supplies the borrowing clause's own note, which 16 of 43 carry. If
resolution needs the gloss then the model is matching our wording rather than
reading the document, and a lookup that only works when we already wrote the
definition is not a lookup.

A SCORING-SET BUG FIXED ALONG THE WAY: the earlier comparison deduped by
clause_id and kept the FIRST run's version, discarding 9 of 40 borrowed symbols
and 6 of the 14 that block a read-back. m0053's two coinages arrive via
defines, not requires/inputs, so an extractor reading only the borrow lists
cannot see them at all. Both corrected, and the reason is recorded where the
extractor lives.

Nothing spent on this commit. Both prompts rendered to resolve_runs/PROMPT_*.txt
with the document elided.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

----END----

commit 467cb836ee8b99c9d159363d91d15b4d45b3efcb
ordinal 125
date 2026-08-08 15:43:45 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject Five prompts for one question, and four of them were fixing my instrument
Can a model tell us where a borrowed predicate's meaning lives in the document?
That is Invariant 1 arm C, whose only recorded objection is "requires the lookup
to exist".

THE SEQUENCE IS THE FINDING, so it is written down in full.

1. Concept map, section-level ($0.0253). 78/78 sections, 165 concepts, 72 of 108
   evidence phrases verbatim. Overlapped what our translator actually coined by
   1 of 32.
2. Predicate-level, pre-registered ($0.0166). Predicted the overlap would rise.
   0 of 32 with 268 candidates. Falsifier fired: prediction is the wrong
   direction, the map is a resolution TARGET not prompt context.
3. Five-solver Haiku panel, free. Unanimous on 2 of 43. `document` counts ranged
   5 to 41 on identical inputs.

   AND THE SPREAD WAS MY FAULT. My prompt asked two different questions in
   adjacent sentences -- "a section establishes what it MEANS" and "a NAME the
   document does not use". Solvers anchored on different ones and both followed
   instructions. Worse, my KEY was name-level while the pipeline needs
   concept-level: all six "coinages" have their concept in the document, and
   interactable_entity is literally "**Assistant**: the entity that the end user
   or developer interacts with". The solvers I scored as wrong were answering
   the more useful question, and the one I called careful had merely shared my
   narrower reading. I reported the opposite before checking.

4. Single solver, concept-level, free. 4/4 on verdict and section. But
   over-resolution MOVED rather than vanished -- 29 `defined-here`, 8 failing
   the prompt's own name test, `absent` used 0 times in 43 -- and the verdict
   was right far more often than the TERM, which is the part the pipeline
   consumes.

   The self-report was worth running and both checkable claims held: the phrase
   it admitted lifting from another section does exist there, and 13 of 41
   resolutions (32%) give a document_term absent from the section cited. It
   independently reached the gap I had already been forced into when I dropped
   pasted_text from the key.

5. Term-first, running. document_term becomes the primary output and the verdict
   falls out of whether one exists, with `described-not-named` added for the 32%
   case and `absent` forced by a required field. The key grows to 5 and spans
   two verdicts, so answering everything the same way cannot score.

Total spend $0.042; the panel work was free because subagent tokens are not API
spend.

Also in this commit: golden_set.py, which built 65 planted items before Matt
pointed out that 58 of them were attached to arbitrary sections -- I had made
the section context load-bearing and then filled it with noise. Superseded by
the panel approach, kept because the taxonomy of linkage kinds in
resolve_runs/TAXONOMY.md is still the right frame for a future test set.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

----END----

commit fbdb92a58e39864690834a5825c234dc5b340a38
ordinal 126
date 2026-08-08 18:55:39 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject resolve: iterate definitions to self-sufficiency, n=5 — consolidation yields nothing
Matt's design: gather passages for a concept, formalize, and if the definition
is not self-sufficient go back for the newly-opened predicates and repeat --
then consolidate across five runs. 8 concepts x 5 runs, bounded at 4 rounds.

This answered the question experiment 5 could not: single-shot formalization
opened 2-3 new undefined predicates per concept, so does the recursion close?

It terminates and the answer is still no. 14 of 40 concept-runs closed. Of 48
round-to-round transitions, 22 shrank, 15 were flat and 11 GREW; five
concept-runs ended with more open than they started, worst [4, 10, 8].

The decisive result is consolidation. Matching rules on (head, body-predicate
set) -- structure, not text -- SIX of eight concepts have ZERO rule shapes
shared by three or more of the five runs. The two that share one share a
body-less ground fact. Borrowed-predicate agreement is 0.00 on all eight;
conflicts_with_later_same_authority accumulated 28 open predicate names with
not one common to all five runs. Defined-head agreement is 0.18 and the five
names every run shares are five of the eight names we supplied in the prompt.
Emergent agreement is zero.

Not a competence failure, which is what makes it a finding: 89% of 205
passages verbatim, clingo accepts 106 of 113 rules, 1 of 40 faked closure.
Iterating makes vocabulary convergence WORSE -- 0.06 single-shot to 0.00 --
because each round coins more names.

Q-6 updated with what this constrains: arm C's lookup cannot be generated,
only seeded from the document's own **Term**: inventory. Not ruled.

Two instrument defects found while scoring, both of which had already produced
a wrong number: the verbatim normaliser did not strip markdown emphasis (76%
reported, 88% true -- third time this instrument has been the broken part, now
DEBUGGING_TIPS 17), and the agreement table scored 0.00 where four of five runs
closed cleanly, because Jaccard over empty sets reads as total disagreement.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjboGhk5XQNsaewwexHvX6

commit 3e10fdf830d61a33a76a7eeb7b0b55a3b6c55f45
ordinal 127
date 2026-08-08 22:20:09 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject resolve: reading the transcripts -- 62% of the iteration was renaming, not resolving
Matt asked why the non-closing concepts did not close. Reading them found the
open-set SIZE metric cannot tell resolving from spinning. task/1 run 5 wrote
three unrelated one-predicate paraphrases in three rounds, each replacing the
last rather than defining what it opened, and open counts [2,2,1] read as
converging.

New measure B2: an open predicate is carried if the next round still owes it or
later defines it, replaced if it vanishes never defined. n=159: carried 61
(38%), REPLACED WITHOUT EVER BEING DEFINED 98 (62%). 27 of 40 concept-runs
dropped an undefined predicate rather than define it.

So the 0.00 agreement headline was measuring two things at once. Classifying
every open predicate in the transcripts gives three causes with three remedies:

(1) genuinely underdetermined by the document -- the spec says an instruction is
superseded if a later one "either contradicts it, overrides it, or otherwise
makes it irrelevant", naming three relations and defining none. Carried by every
run that reaches them, closed by none. This is the finding worth having.

(2) missing pipeline metadata, NOT a document gap -- seven predicates about
section authority, opened while quoting the document saying every section IS
assigned an authority level. The document states it; the corpus does not carry
it. Ours to fix.

(3) situation vocabulary the prompt failed to fix -- my defect. message/1,
role/2, message_order/2 are exactly what the prompt named primitive. Run 2
declared them primitive, run 3 left them open. The prompt gave a criterion and
no list, so the runs drew the bottom of the formalization in different places.

A meaningful part of the 0.00 is (2) and (3). A fair re-run needs the situation
vocabulary as a fixed primitive list, section authority on the corpus, and a
driver that pins the open set so a round cannot discharge a predicate by
paraphrasing the head. Only what survives that is evidence about the document.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjboGhk5XQNsaewwexHvX6

----END----

commit 39110f6ed119cb730fe5095790c9f7e5ec509b24
ordinal 128
date 2026-08-08 22:36:21 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject resolve: section agreement is a ROUND-1 phenomenon and iterating only adds disagreement
Matt asked whether the single-concept multi-turn runs found the same supporting
sections. Measured across the same 8 concepts, five runs each:

  single-turn retrieval (subset_run1..5): all-5 9, union 14, agreement 0.64
                                          5 of 8 concepts UNANIMOUS at 1.00
  multi-turn iterative (iter_run1..5):    all-5 7, union 24, agreement 0.29

So yes, they typically find the same sections -- retrieval was never the weak
link. Multi-turn made it worse, and the by-round split says how:

  round 1 alone   in all 5: 7   union:  9   agreement 0.78
  round 2 alone   in all 5: 3   union: 10   agreement 0.30
  round 3 alone   in all 5: 0   union:  3   agreement 0.00
  cumulative      in all 5: 7 / 7 / 7 / 7   union: 9 / 19 / 24 / 24

The all-5 column NEVER MOVES after round 1. Fifteen sections are added across
rounds 2-4 and not one is found by all five runs.

Not a retrieval defect. Round 1 asks all five runs the same question and they
converge at 0.78. Rounds 2+ ask what defines the predicates each run itself
opened, and those agree at 0.00. The later rounds retrieve competently against
five different questions -- the loop manufactures the divergence it propagates.

Added as iter_score.py section F2 so it is reproducible rather than asserted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjboGhk5XQNsaewwexHvX6

commit 7ffa78f190b3d2058558ff8a07f05e1c27bbc8fc
ordinal 129
date 2026-08-08 22:51:53 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject resolve: extensional identity -- right idea, but stored data measures clause provenance
Matt's proposal: stop defining borrowed predicates, let a concept's identity be
the region of document text it is grounded in. Names pointing at the same text
are one concept; relations fall out of set algebra. The measurements favour it --
it builds on section retrieval (0.78, the only signal that survived repetition)
and discards vocabulary (0.06 -> 0.00, which never did), and it is statically
checkable in a way no definition was.

extension_id.py tests it over solver_v4.json, 41 predicates with locatable
verbatim excerpts. It does not survive contact:

  character-Jaccard 1.00      5 pairs, 5 share a borrowing clause (100%)
  0.8+                        1 pair,  1 (100%)
  0.5+                        8 pairs, 8 (100%)
  any overlap                31 pairs, 26 (84%)
  baseline over all 820      104 (13%)

Similarity is measuring provenance. The resolver was told which clause wanted
each predicate, so it cited that clause's home passage for every predicate the
clause borrows. includes_malicious_instructions and not_read_carefully score
1.00 because both are m0105's.

Worse, interactable_entity/1 and interaction_entity/1 -- m0053's twins, the exact
defect Q-6 names -- have no locatable extension at all, so the method is silent
on the case it exists for. And the one real cross-clause synonym pair
(transformation_of_user_content m0255 / translation_of_user_content m0150) merges
at section granularity and separates at span granularity: the granularity that
removes the confound destroys the signal.

Two instrument defects fixed here as well, both of which had already produced
output: any-overlap identity is dominated by how much text a model chose to
quote, and union-find takes the transitive closure of overlap, chaining
unrelated names into one 8-member blob. Together they made a containment table
whose 16 pairs shared a right-hand side 15 times. Now character-Jaccard, no
chaining.

Pre-registers the clause-blind retrieval experiment with five predictions and
names P1 and P4 as the falsifiers, per the sandwich rule.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjboGhk5XQNsaewwexHvX6

----END----

commit de3912246d6051ffd25a82fecc9f2516ba794296
ordinal 130
date 2026-08-08 22:56:25 -0700
author Matt Stults
subject resolve: the blind corpus had the answer key printed in it -- three runs void
The clause-blind experiment was dispatched against DOCUMENT.txt, which is not
the document. It is the document with a needs_block injected under every section
marker -- 78 of them -- each reading "[BORROWED PREDICATES -- the rules written
from this section test these...]" followed by the predicate names. The file
handed out as the blind corpus was a complete name-to-section answer key,
printed above the text it was meant to hide.

Caught by luck, not by a check: a subagent's prose report mentioned finding a
name "listed in the BORROWED PREDICATES section of
follow_all_applicable_instructions". Nothing in the JSON would have shown it,
and the results would have read as a strong positive -- near-perfect grounding,
high agreement, exactly what the experiment wanted to find.

The generalisable form, recorded as DEBUGGING_TIPS 18: an artifact built for one
experiment carries that experiment's framing, and the framing is often the next
experiment's answer. DOCUMENT.txt was correct for resolve_probe.py, whose whole
question was "given that this section borrows these names, where are they
established?" Reusing it for a question that must not know the borrower inverted
its meaning without changing a byte.

Adds DOCUMENT_CLEAN.txt: needs-blocks stripped, 121 lines dropped, all 78
sections intact, zero residual predicate/arity tokens (the one grep hit is a
Creative Commons URL). Three leaked runs deleted rather than kept and labelled,
since both leaked and clean runs write blind_run<N>.json and a stale file a
scorer globs up is indistinguishable from a real result.

Still to build: a clean-corpus assertion in the dispatch path. Today it is a
documented manual step, which is the transcript-only procedure REPRODUCIBILITY.md
calls a review finding.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjboGhk5XQNsaewwexHvX6
